extracted.intended_audience: business news readers and corporate/PR professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and evaluative criteria for corporate crisis public-relations response (illustrated by BP's Gulf oil spill). Focuses on what companies should do and avoid when managing major environmental/operational crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show human compassion
rubrics_metrics.description: All crises are personal. Action and sacrifice is absolutely critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate empathy and human concern publicly — e.g., executives visibly helping crews, wearing hard hats and life vests. Avoid appearing detached or purely managerial; human gestures matter to public perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the company's own spill/damage-control plan
rubrics_metrics.description: BP hasn't followed its own internal guidelines for damage control after a spill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to pre-filed emergency/PR playbooks. Deviation from internal prescriptions undermines credibility and invites criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make promises to restore property or ecology to 'normal'
rubrics_metrics.description: Company spill plan: 'No statement shall be made containing any of the following: promises that property, ecology or anything else will be restored to normal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid categorical guarantees about full restoration; such promises can be unrealistic and contradict internal rules. Public ad pledges claiming 'we will make this right' can violate guidance and raise legal/credibility issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put senior executives visibly involved (action and sacrifice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggested putting CEO in a hard hat and life vest, helping crews contain and clean up the spill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visible leadership participation signals commitment. Even if uncomfortable, participation (hands-on presence) helps show accountability and dedication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be culturally sensitive about spokesperson selection
rubrics_metrics.description: It might have been more appropriate for senior U.S. executives to take the heat; foreign leaders may not be best-suited in certain national contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider local culture/traditions when choosing who represents the company in-country. A mismatch (e.g., a foreign CEO leading U.S. response) can inflame sentiment and reduce effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tone-deaf personal remarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Insensitive comments (example: CEO's 'I'd like my life back') upset victims and look out of touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train spokespeople to avoid self-centered or flippant comments. Even offhand lines can dominate coverage and damage empathy-based messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest and consistent about technical/scientific facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives quibbled about existence of undersea plumes, downplayed damage, and issued conflicting statements about concentrations and timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide accurate, clear, and consistent scientific/technical information. Avoid minimizing or qualifying facts in ways that later require walkbacks; contradictions erode trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid optimistic or speculative timelines for resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: BP made far-too-optimistic predictions for when the spill could be stopped (e.g., 'relative trickle' soon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from setting firm public timelines unless confident. Overly optimistic projections that prove false harm credibility; frame uncertainty candidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize fixing the problem over image management
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Crisis management is about fixing the problem. It's not about looking good.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate resources first to containment, cleanup, and victim relief rather than image-focused advertising. The only reliable route to reputation repair is solving the underlying issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tangible financial/operational gestures of solidarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions included cutting gas prices at stations along the Gulf Coast as a show of financial solidarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider concrete measures that help affected communities (discounts, direct aid, expedited claims). Tangible actions often speak louder than words or ads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide accessible, useful information to affected people
rubrics_metrics.description: BP bought search ads linking to oil-response sites to help people find forms and contacts quickly and effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make recovery resources, claims forms, and contact points highly visible and easy to access. However, be aware such efforts can be perceived as brand-protecting unless clearly focused on relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be transparent and allow media access and questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Early daily in-person briefings allowed questions; later teleconferences limited questions and access, which drew criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit open briefings, field questions, and reasonable media visits. Overly controlling access or limiting questions creates suspicion and suggests hiding information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid tightly controlling media access in ways that appear secretive
rubrics_metrics.description: BP restricted media visits to 'rooms that are shown' and limited interactions, arguing staff must do 'day job.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While protecting operational work is legitimate, excessive control of what reporters see or who they can talk to fosters mistrust. Balance operational security with openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate spokesperson roles to prevent mixed messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Confusion arose when different executives (Hayward, Suttles) made overlapping or conflicting public statements; aides complained about spotlight-stealing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define spokesperson hierarchy and messaging protocols. Ensure interviews and public statements are coordinated to present a unified, consistent narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using PR advertising as a substitute for direct relief spending
rubrics_metrics.description: BP aired multimillion-dollar ads pledging to 'make this right,' prompting criticism (including from the President) that money should go to cleanup and compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that high-profile ad buys during an ongoing disaster can be seen as misprioritization. Direct relief and compensation typically improve reputation more than advertising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address shareholder-versus-victim optics carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate over whether BP should pay its dividend during the crisis; lawmakers insisted victims come before shareholders, while retirees depended on dividends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize and manage perceptions about financial decisions (dividends, payouts) during crises. Transparent rationale and prioritization of victims can reduce reputational backlash.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge evolving severity and adapt messaging accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimates of the spill's severity grew by the week; BP often appeared to downplay early on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Update the public as new data emerge; acknowledge uncertainty and adjust communications rather than sticking to earlier minimized assessments.
